title: Phoenix Snow Park: A Beginner's Guide to Pyeongchang's Olympic Ski Resort
html:
If you want to try skiing or snowboarding in Korea and you're willing to go a little further from Seoul for a bigger resort, Phoenix Snow Park (also called Phoenix Park) in Pyeongchang is one of the country's best-known options — it's a full-size mountain resort that even hosted events at the 2018 Winter Olympics. Here's what the resort is like, when the 2026/27 season runs, and how to get there and get set up for your first day on snow.

What Is Phoenix Snow Park?

Phoenix Snow Park sits in Bongpyeong-myeon, a rural township in Pyeongchang County, Gangwon State — the same mountain region that hosted the 2018 PyeongChang Winter Olympics. The resort has around 21 slopes for every skill level, served by eight lifts, six slow-moving conveyor belts (easy "escalators" for the beginner slope and ski school area), and a scenic gondola that carries you up to Montblanc Peak at about 1,050 meters. You don't have to ski to ride the gondola — plenty of visitors go up just for the mountain view. The resort is also attached to a hotel and condo complex, so it's easy to turn a ski day into an overnight trip if you want more time on the slopes.

Photo: Phoenix Snow Park, via Korea Tourism Organization's official TourAPI data.

2026/27 Season: Opening Dates and Lift Tickets

Korea's ski resorts open based on snow and temperature, not a fixed calendar date, so dates shift a little every year. For the 2026/27 season, Phoenix Snow Park was aiming to open its first runs around late November 2026, with the full resort (and Seoul shuttle buses) running from late November through early March. Because an opening date announced in October or November can still move a few days depending on weather, always check the resort's own site or your booking platform for the confirmed opening status before you travel.

Lift ticket prices also change by season and by day (weekday vs. weekend, daytime vs. night skiing), so rather than quoting a number that may already be outdated by the time you read this, book through the official Phoenix Park / Phoenix Pyeongchang website for the current price, or through an English-language platform like Trazy, Klook, or KKday, which sell lift-ticket packages (sometimes bundled with gear rental and a shuttle bus) with English checkout and customer support. A multi-day season pass is also available if you're planning more than one trip in a season, but full-day single tickets are the better option for a first visit.

First Time Skiing? Lessons, Rentals, and the Beginner Zone

You don't need any of your own gear to try skiing or snowboarding here. The resort has a rental counter at the base where staff fit you with skis or a snowboard, boots, a helmet, and poles, and separately rents warm snow clothing (jacket, pants, gloves) if you didn't bring your own — just tell them your height, weight, and shoe size and they'll fit you on the spot. Beginner group and private lessons are available too, often sold as a combo with your lift ticket and rental gear through the same travel platforms mentioned above, which is the easiest way to book everything in English before you even land in Korea.

Phoenix Snow Park's ski school slope is served by those gentle conveyor belts instead of a regular chairlift, so total beginners can practice standing, turning, and stopping without needing to get on and off a moving lift right away. If you've genuinely never clipped into skis before, ask for this beginner area specifically when you arrive.

Not Skiing? Sledding and Other Things to Do

If part of your group doesn't want to ski, Phoenix Snow Park still has plenty for them. The resort's snow village area includes a dedicated snow sledding hill that's separate from the ski slopes — no lessons or experience needed, you just sit on a sled and go. Some day-tour packages from Seoul also add a stop at a nearby Daegwallyeong sheep farm on the way, which is a popular add-on for families or travelers mixing skiing with a gentler side trip. Riding the gondola up to Montblanc Peak (mentioned above) is another good non-ski option if someone in your group just wants the view and some fresh mountain air.

Getting There From Seoul Without a Car

Phoenix Snow Park is roughly 2.5 to 3.5 hours from central Seoul, and it isn't on a subway or train line, so most foreign visitors book a round-trip shuttle bus through a platform like Trazy, Klook, KKday, or iVisitKorea. These buses typically pick up near stations like Hongik University, Sinchon, or Myeongdong in the morning and return to Seoul in the evening, and some routes transfer passengers to a second bus partway through the trip — staff are on hand to help if that happens to your bus. A few important details: the shuttle driver usually doesn't speak English, so double-check the destination sign on the bus before boarding, and the bus will not wait for latecomers, so arrive at your pickup point early.

💡 How locals actually do it: Many Korean skiers buy their lift ticket and gear rental together through the resort's own app a day or two ahead of time, since online prices are usually cheaper than paying at the counter and it skips the ticket-window line entirely on busy weekend mornings.
